\paragraph{Probing Methodology and Layer Selection.}
Causal abstraction~\cite{geiger2025causal} formalizes when high-level causal models faithfully describe neural computation, grounding use of internal representations. Linear probing spans layer-wise classifiers~\cite{alain2017understanding}, sentence probing~\cite{conneau2018probing}, and surveys~\cite{belinkov2019analysis,belinkov2022probing,rogers2020primer}. Control tasks~\cite{hewitt2019control} distinguish structure from memorization (we adopt these; \cref{app:control}). Information-theoretic and causal formulations address probe complexity~\cite{voita2020information,pimentel2020information,ravfogel2020null,ravfogel2022rlace,belrose2023leace,elazar2021amnesic}. \citet{marks2024geometry} find emergent linear structure in LLM truth representations, consistent with our safety commitment separability. Most directly, \citet{boxo2025linear_probes} show linear probes can rely on textual evidence rather than deeper representations, motivating our controlled HS-vs-text comparison; \citet{alvarez2026transport_geometry} apply hidden-state geometry to step-level hallucination detection concurrently with our work. Despite this foundation, layer selection remains underexamined: most studies select by a single metric without sensitivity analysis, a practice we show can reverse conclusions (\cref{sec:layer-results}). Our approach is correlational; causal validation~\citep{geiger2025causal,belrose2023leace,li2024iti} is needed to confirm probed directions are causally active.

\paragraph{Probing Methodology and Layer Selection.}
Causal abstraction~\cite{geiger2025causal} formalizes when high-level causal models faithfully describe neural computation, grounding use of internal representations. Linear probing spans layer-wise classifiers~\cite{alain2017understanding}, sentence probing~\cite{conneau2018probing}, and surveys~\cite{belinkov2019analysis,belinkov2022probing,rogers2020primer}. Control tasks~\cite{hewitt2019control} distinguish structure from memorization (we adopt these; \cref{app:control}). Information-theoretic and causal formulations address probe complexity~\cite{voita2020information,pimentel2020information,ravfogel2020null,ravfogel2022rlace,belrose2023leace,elazar2021amnesic}. \citet{marks2024geometry} find emergent linear structure in LLM truth representations, consistent with our safety commitment separability. That information distributes non-uniformly across layers is well established: \citet{tenney2019bert} show syntactic information concentrates in early layers while semantic information peaks later, and \citet{jawahar2019bert} confirm this hierarchy through probing and attention analysis. Our contribution is orthogonal: the known layer-wise information gradient interacts with metric choice to produce systematic selection bias in safety probes, a phenomenon not previously characterized. Most directly, \citet{boxo2025linear_probes} show linear probes can rely on textual evidence rather than deeper representations; our metric bias analysis provides a complementary mechanism: shallow-layer probes exploit compressed representations that inflate crossing rate, a geometric effect consistent with text-leakage at layers where representations have not yet diverged from surface features. \citet{alvarez2026transport_geometry} apply hidden-state geometry to step-level hallucination detection concurrently with our work. Despite this foundation, layer selection remains underexamined: most studies select by a single metric without sensitivity analysis, a practice we show can reverse conclusions (\cref{sec:layer-results}). Our approach is correlational; causal validation~\citep{geiger2025causal,belrose2023leace,li2024iti} is needed to confirm probed directions are causally active.

tool_args.old_string: Existing safety detectors target fundamentally different problems. Hidden-state (HS) methods such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} classify adversarial inputs at the token level, while text monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} scan generated reasoning for explicit violations. Neither tracks the gradual, multi-step commitment process. A fundamental question remains: should a monitoring system read the model's hidden states or its generated text? This comparison has never been conducted under controlled conditions, and a further complication is that HS probes require selecting which transformer layer to monitor. Layer selection is a researcher degree of freedom whose metric sensitivity has received almost no scrutiny, yet we show it can reverse a study's central conclusion.
tool_args.new_string: Existing safety detectors target fundamentally different problems. Hidden-state (HS) methods such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} classify adversarial inputs at the token level, while text monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} scan generated reasoning for explicit violations. Neither tracks the gradual, multi-step commitment process. A practical question is whether a monitoring system should read the model's hidden states or its generated text, but the reliability of HS safety probes depends on methodological choices that have not been systematically examined. Chief among these is layer selection: HS probes require choosing which transformer layer to monitor, a researcher degree of freedom whose metric sensitivity has received almost no scrutiny. We show it can reverse a study's central conclusion.

tool_args.new_string: \paragraph{Layer selection stability (LOO-CV).} Leave-one-out cross-validation on the validation set shows moderate consistency for 7--8B models (65--68\% dominant-layer agreement) but lower for 32B, confirming that layer selection instability is particularly acute at small sample sizes. Under pure balanced accuracy, the dominant layer is selected in 68\% (QwQ-32B: L30, 13/19 folds) and 65\% (R1-32B: L47, 13/20 folds) of folds. Alternative selections scatter across neighboring layers (L29, L55--56 for QwQ; L32, L38, L43 for R1-32B), reinforcing the need for multi-metric auditing rather than single-metric layer selection. Threshold-dependent metrics show tighter convergence to L63 for both 32B models.

1	Reasoning models with chain-of-thought (CoT) can self-jailbreak: their reasoning traces transition from safe deliberation to committed harmful generation without adversarial input. Detecting the commitment point (CP), the reasoning step after which a model's chain of thought becomes irreversibly committed to an unsafe conclusion, requires monitoring internal representations or generated text. We study four reasoning LLMs on the HarmThoughts safety-probing benchmark and show that the outcome of this comparison depends critically on which transformer layer is monitored. A biased composite metric masks the hidden-state (HS) advantage at 32B scale by selecting shallow layers where representation compression inflates threshold crossings. Principled layer selection recovers significant HS precision gains in three of four models (+19.2 to +21.9pp, Holm-Bonferroni corrected); the fourth model's (R1-32B) advantage is position-mediated (residualized gap below minimum detectable effect). Encoder quality bounds the advantage: against a stronger 1024-dimensional text encoder, only 1/4 models survives correction. Layer selection sensitivity is the robust methodological finding; the empirical HS advantage is conditional, and current probes characterize the commitment phenomenon rather than constitute production detectors.
